source.title: An OV-Coherent Toy Model of Attention Head Superposition

record.tranche_reason: The post reports toy-model results on attention-head interference and argues that this behavior may differ from traditional feature superposition; the author later agrees that polysemanticity, distributed representation, and interference alone are insufficient to establish true superposition.
record.gate_note: The post reports qualitative attention and logit behaviors, dimension configurations, and perfect accuracy on a signal-only test set. It explicitly says sparsity and importance were not varied. The comments include a proposed simpler solution and the author's response; cited results from other work are not recorded as findings.
record.test_reason: The post studies interference and distributed computation across attention heads in a 1-layer attention-only toy task. It does not measure features stored as nearly orthogonal directions in fewer dimensions, vary sparsity or importance, measure neuron polysemanticity, or study SAEs or feature dimensionality. Head-level 'superposition' of skip-trigrams is a related but different construct. In the comments, the author concedes the result is likely not 'true' superposition. That is a discussion point, not a result bearing on V3, which concerns neurons.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with two additions. The post claims the task shows heads performing 'computation in superposition', driven by a new OV-coherent incentive, via reversed preference orderings and constructive interference. In the comments, the author later concedes this was likely not true superposition and calls the work less interesting in retrospect. They still find the inverted-preference and context-inference behaviours interesting.
record.recipe_differences: This is a 1-layer attention-only toy task involving multiple source tokens and conditional dependence between QK and OV circuits, rather than the original Toy Models of Superposition setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The post reports split attention only for d_head < 3, discusses orthogonal token storage for d_head >= 3, and reports one-head solutions for d_head >= 4. It says the flipped-hierarchy pattern was overwhelmingly more common, but does not give counts.

fits_no_version.finding: In a 2-head attention-only toy model, heads learn reversed preference orderings over signal tokens. Conditional OV outputs then constructively interfere on the correct completion.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attention heads can coordinate QK preference orderings and conditional OV outputs to compute nonlinear functions of multiple source tokens (head-level interference / 'attention head superposition').

fits_no_version.finding: Perfect accuracy holds even at d_head = 1 with 2 heads, and with 1 head at d_head >= 4. Split attention appears only at d_head < 3.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The task solution depends on a trade-off between head dimension and head count ('bottleneck superposition'), which is speculative.

record.problems: The post says it did not vary sparsity or importance and that its analysis was not exhaustive. It gives qualitative descriptions rather than quantitative geometric measurements, and reports no uncertainty estimates.

untested.parts: Sparsity and importance were not varied; no feature-direction geometry was measured; no phase transition was examined.
Neuron polysemanticity and capacity allocation by importance were not studied.
Only a commenter's argument, accepted by the author, that interference or distributed representation is not superposition. No neuron-level test.
No LLMs or SAEs; the IOI work is mentioned only as abandoned or future work.
Feature dimensionality was not measured; orthogonal storage of tokens is speculation.

record.verdict_notes: The record over-links rows to V1 and V6 and gives limits_scope labels without any measurement of the V1 or V6 constructs. All rows have been reassigned to none. The author's reply says the n_heads = 2, d_head >= 4 model still prefers the hierarchy solution over the simpler one-head-style solution. The reply also suggests the plots were from a variant other than the d_head = 5 one the post names, which is ambiguous.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not vary sparsity or feature importance, establish a sparsity-dependent transition, or comprehensively measure feature-direction geometry.
It does not test neuron polysemanticity or whether feature importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
The author agrees that interference or distributed representation alone is insufficient evidence of true superposition, but the study does not test polysemantic neurons arising for other reasons.
LLMs and SAE-recovered features are not studied; possible relevance to real models is speculation.
The post discusses scalar head dimensions and orthogonal storage of signal tokens, but does not comprehensively establish the dimensionality of the represented features.

rows.subject: 2-head model
rows.operation_detail: Inspected QK attention preference orderings over signal tokens.

conditions.value: two signal tokens in the context; final token 0

rows.measure: Attention preference ordering and whether the two signal tokens are both attended to.
rows.value: Both heads learned strict preference orderings, generally reversed; the example orders were 2, 3, 4, 1 and 1, 4, 3, 2. The post says this ensures both signal tokens are fully attended to.
rows.note: This reports distributed attention across heads, not a direct measurement of nearly orthogonal feature directions.
rows.check: Reversed QK preference orderings across heads are head-level task distribution, not feature directions in a lower-dimensional space, so the row does not bear on V1.

rows.subject: 2-head model
rows.operation_detail: Inspected each head's direct logit contributions conditional on its attended signal token.
rows.measure: Whether head contributions to completion logits constructively interfere on the correct output.
rows.value: The heads contribute to multiple completions in some contexts; the post reports that only the correct completion receives positive contributions from both heads in the described example.
rows.note: Qualitative evidence of head-level interference; not a measure of the feature-direction geometry asserted by V1.
rows.check: Constructive logit interference between heads is not the V1 construct: no feature geometry and no sparsity transition.

rows.subject: models with d_head < 3
rows.operation_detail: Inspected learned attention patterns in models with smaller head dimensions.
rows.measure: Whether heads used split attention or the flipped-hierarchy scheme.
rows.value: The post says split attention was seen only for d_head < 3.
rows.note: Attention pattern alone does not determine whether represented features are one-dimensional or multidimensional.
rows.check: Split attention at d_head < 3 is an attention-pattern observation and says nothing about whether features are 1-D. It is also unquantified ('overwhelmingly more common', no counts).

rows.measure: Orthogonality of signal-token representations in the head dimension.
rows.value: The author says the absence of split attention at these dimensions supports the idea that signal tokens can be stored orthogonally.
rows.locator: Future Work - Toy Models; Split attention model, d_head bottlenecks, and the surprising resourcefulness of networks

relation.reason: The post discusses and proposes attention-head superposition, but its measurements do not test the catalog's versions or use an established finding as a tool.

tranche.reason: The results concern attention allocation, conditional logit interference and task solvability. They do not establish any listed claim version; orthogonal storage is speculative, and sparsity and importance were not varied.

source_check.notes: The later author response accepts that distributed representation and interference are insufficient to establish true superposition. The pack truncates some row values; the visible claims are supported, but omitted wording cannot be independently checked.
